extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students/scholars of classical drama and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria (from commentary on Aristotle's Poetics) for composing and evaluating tragic drama: appropriate subjects, character types, plot shape, and the emotional effects tragedy must produce (pity, fear, catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of tragedy / catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy aims to refine the passions by exciting pity and fear, producing Terror, Compassion, and Pleasure, and thereby purging the Passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a representation does not excite pity and fear, and therefore does not produce those Effects (terror, compassion, pleasure), 'it is most certain that it can never obtain its end, and purge the Passions.' A piece that fails to produce these effects cannot properly be called Tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude very virtuous protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: The misfortunes of a very virtuous man 'cannot naturally excite in us, either Fear or Pity, because they give us Horror.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle therefore excludes a very virtuous man from Tragedy: martyrdom or the sufferings of the supremely virtuous cannot refine the passions because the audience is thrown into despair or horror rather than pity. Example/anti-pattern: Corneille's Polyeuctes (martyrdom) is criticized as an improper tragic subject for this reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude very wicked protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: The misfortunes of a very wicked man will produce neither Fear nor Pity and may instead produce indignation or even pleasure at just punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting the prosperity of the wicked nourishes and strengthens vice ('There is nothing more opposite to the Refining of the Passions, than the prosperity of the Wicked'); thus a tragic subject should not make the wicked prosper, nor hinge the plot on punishing villains as the tragic center, since that does not refine the audience's passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist should be neither wholly good nor wholly bad (the just mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero ought to be 'neither good nor bad' — a mixture of virtue and vice (the 'just mean').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an exactly balanced character cannot be found, choose one 'rather good than wicked.' Such mixed characters can arouse both pity and fear; examples discussed include Oedipus (a mix of virtues and vices) and the praise of Racine's Phedra as closer to the rule. Avoid making the hero purely innocent or purely villainous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fall should result from an involuntary fault (hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The misfortune of the tragic hero should arise from an involuntary fault — an error committed by ignorance, imprudence, transport of passion, or external compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's examples: Oedipus's error of ignorance or transport of passion, Thyestes' action tied to anger, and other cases where the fault is involuntary or forced. The text distinguishes actions considered voluntary in moral analysis from the poetic/general treatment where such passion-driven acts may be represented as involuntary for tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple (single) plot preferred to double catastrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-composed fable ought to be simple and not double; a double fable with two opposite catastrophes (a happy ending for the good and an unhappy one for the wicked) is opposed to Aristotle's rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A double catastrophe undermines tragedy because 'the prosperity of the Good hath nothing Tragical in it' and the punishment of the wicked does not produce the pity/fear catharsis. Example of double structure: Sophocles' Electra (happy and unhappy outcomes combined) is given as the kind of structure Aristotle rejects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy represents a universal fable (imitation of mankind)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragedy is 'an Universal Fable' that regards mankind in general; changing the names (mutato nomine) does not change its universal nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although poets often use the names of eminent persons to make the action noble and credible, the poet's aim is to represent human nature; the particular names add magnificence but the underlying fable must be general and recognizable to all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use eminent names to render action magnificent and credible
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of persons of great fortune and reputation are used to make the action appear great and more credible; the greatness of the person renders the action great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy does not require that the action itself be inherently important; using princes or great men as figures of the universal fable makes the plot appear noble. This answers the objection that tragedy must only concern ordinary people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not portray the wicked prospering (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying the prosperity of the wicked is counterproductive: 'instead of correcting, it nourishes and strengthens them' and removes motive for self-correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragic poet should avoid making wicked characters successful in ways that would encourage vice. If the wicked prosper, the audience will not be moved to reform, and the play fails its moral/psychological purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience relatability — make high-status figures 'like ourselves'
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Kings and eminent persons appear on stage, their passions and misfortunes must be presented so that the audience can identify and fear similar errors — 'kings and princes were like ourselves' in passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objection that tragedies of great persons wouldn't produce fear is answered by showing that the passions (ambition, fear, hatred, revenge) are common human features; the spectator judges that even a king who yields to such passions deserves pity. Thus rank may be used without losing relatability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subjects that allow the correction of specific passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose tragic subjects whose incidents and character flaws instruct the audience about particular vices (e.g., anger, curiosity) that ought to be corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thyestes/Atreus illustrate choleric revenge and its perils; Oedipus exemplifies curiosity and violent temper. The tragic example should enable the audience to recognize and correct those passions in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic/general treatment vs. moral/particular analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's analysis in Poetics treats actions in the gross for poetic effect, while moral treatises examine actions individually and in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent contradictions (e.g., whether acts of anger are voluntary) are resolved by recognizing differing aims: poetry permits treating passion-driven acts as forced/involuntary for tragic purposes, whereas ethics scrutinizes voluntariness case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/audience taste consideration in subject choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The changing taste and critical capacity of the audience affect which subjects succeed: 'now their Relish is more delicate' and only plays conforming to Aristotelian rules tend to be esteemed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author should be aware that what once pleased a less critical audience may no longer succeed; choosing subjects and shaping them according to the rules (mixed characters, simple plots, proper cathartic effects) aligns with modern-critical tastes as Aristotle observes.
